blocks.label: Smooth pressure, turning wheels
blocks.content: In a quiet, open space, roll at walking pace and squeeze both brake levers gradually. Feel the bike slow without a lurch. Keep your fingers on the bars and your eyes ahead. The aim is a controlled stop with both wheels still turning until the last moment. If a wheel skids or the bike pitches abruptly, reset at a lower speed and use less lever pressure. Brake sound is not a reliable measure of grip; feel what the tires and bike are doing.

blocks.title: A corner arrives sooner than expected
blocks.content: A rider approaches a gravel bend and notices a loose patch near the entry. The useful decision happens before the bend: look where the bike needs to go, reduce speed while the bike is relatively upright, and leave room to change the line. Grabbing a lever after leaning into the loose patch asks the tires to slow and turn at the same time. The lesson is to give yourself time and space, not to hit a particular speed or brake-force split.

### What the brakes can and cannot do

Both brakes help slow a bicycle. As you decelerate, load shifts toward the front wheel, so the front brake can contribute a great deal of stopping force. That does not make it an on/off switch, and it does not make the rear brake disposable. Squeeze both levers gradually and adjust to the grip you feel.

Loose gravel, wet clay, sand, bumps, tire setup, and gradient can all change how the bike responds. No table can tell you the stopping distance for the next bend. Give yourself more room than you think you need, especially when you cannot see the exit or the surface changes.

Set a comfortable speed before a turn when you can. If you still need to slow while turning, make the input gentle and leave extra room. The goal is to avoid abrupt braking or steering, not to obey a rule that forbids touching the brakes mid-corner.

items.title: Why braking and turning compete for grip
items.content:
A tire has limited grip on any given patch of ground. Braking and turning both ask for some of it. How much is available changes from moment to moment, so a numerical “traction budget” cannot set a safe speed.

In practice, look through the turn, slow early on the straighter approach, then steer with light hands. If the surface changes or the bike feels unsettled, reduce your demands on the tires and make room for a wider, slower line. Never treat a calculated number as permission to ride faster.

blocks.title: The Braking Sequence
blocks.description: A short checklist for a bend you can see clearly. Slow down sooner when visibility or grip is uncertain.

steps.detail: Find the bend, the exit, and any loose or wet patches. Keep enough room to stop within what you can see.
While the bike is mostly upright, squeeze both brakes smoothly. Start sooner when the surface is unfamiliar.
As the bike leans, reduce heavy braking. If you need more slowing, be gentle and allow a wider line.
Keep your eyes on the open path and let the bike settle before adding speed.

blocks.title: The Braking Sequence — brake, release, look through
blocks.alt: Illustrated Gravel God rider with sequential callouts for braking on the approach, easing brake pressure at turn-in, and looking through the corner.
blocks.caption: This is an illustrated sequence, not riding footage. Practice smooth braking on a flat, traffic-free loop. The lesson also includes a real-rider demonstration.

blocks.title: Smooth-Stop Practice
blocks.description: Practice progressive use of both brakes on a flat, traffic-free stretch with a clear runout. Wear a helmet and check that the brakes work before starting. Stay at a speed from which you can stop comfortably; stop the drill if the surface, bike, or your control feels uncertain.

variants.label: Flat-ground stops
steps: Mark a start and a generous stopping area on flat, clean ground away from traffic and other riders.
Roll at walking pace. Look ahead and squeeze both levers gradually until you stop.
Repeat only while each stop feels calm and both wheels track straight. Notice whether either lever makes the bike lurch or skid.
Move the start a little farther away if you want more practice time; do not chase a shorter stopping distance.

variants.label: Approach a visible bend
steps: Choose a wide, familiar, low-speed bend with a clear exit and no traffic.
On the straight approach, use both brakes smoothly to reach a speed that feels easy to steer.
Ease off strong braking as you begin to turn. Look through the exit and leave room for a wider line.
If you need to slow further, do so gently and stop the exercise if grip feels uncertain.

proof_gate.description: You can repeat several calm stops and low-speed turns without a skid, abrupt lever grab, or need to rescue the line.
proof_gate.target: Consistent control at a comfortable speed, with no speed or braking-count target

blocks.title: If a wheel starts to skid

scenarios.label: Wheel lock during a practice stop
scenarios.situation: A tire stops rolling while the bicycle is still moving.
steps: Ease pressure on the brake that locked so the wheel can roll again. Avoid a sudden squeeze on the other lever.
Look ahead, keep the bike as upright as the space allows, and allow a longer runout.
Stop the session. Check tire grip, brake function, and your approach speed before deciding whether to practice again.

scenarios.label: Unsettled bike in a bend
scenarios.situation: The tire feels as if it is pushing or the line is running wide.
steps: Look toward the open space and avoid abrupt braking or steering.
Reduce the demands you are placing on the tires; allow the bike a wider path if there is safe room.
After stopping safely, choose a slower entry and more room on the next attempt. If you cannot see a safe line, end the drill.

blocks.content:
### Your braking notes

After practice, write down the surface, weather, tire setup, and what a calm stop felt like. Note where you began slowing before a familiar bend. These are observations from your bike and your hands, not a promised stopping distance for race day. A new surface or different weather calls for another conservative check.

blocks.title: How To Brake In Any Situation | MTB Skills
blocks.caption: Front and rear braking demonstrated — see the weight shift and modulation.

blocks.question: You approach a visible gravel bend and notice loose stones near the entry. What is the best first move?

options.text: Look through the bend and slow smoothly with both brakes while the bike is mostly upright
Keep speed and rely on a fixed corner-speed calculation
Use only one brake so the other tire keeps all its grip
Wait until the bike is leaned over, then grab both levers hard

blocks.explanation: Create time and room before the turn. Squeeze both brakes gradually while mostly upright, then ease heavy braking as you steer. The right entry speed depends on the grip and visibility you have.

blocks.content: Before the next lesson, do one short Smooth-Stop Practice session in a flat, traffic-free space. Write down what progressive pressure on both levers felt like. Keep the speed low enough that every stop remains unhurried.
In Cornering Without Clenching, you will carry the same habit into a bend. Look ahead, enter at a speed you can manage, and leave room when the surface changes.
